posts.name: Wendell
posts.cooked:
Hey, welcome! 

I am Spanish too, and quite new to this forum (I think this is my third post). It seems that people is starting to know this game here... 
(Well, "here", I live in Berlin, but you know what I mean..)

I got the game in December, but I had already been trying to find it for a couple of months. It was really hard for me to find. Of course, I moved to Berlin in September, and I speak very litle German, so it made the task harder. I also was busy with far less important things, like finding a job and doing all the paperwork in the world. At the end I also bought it online (in http://www.shop4de.com). 

So far, every time I have shown this game to new players, they have loved it. Even people who are not into comics, or have no experience with this kind of card games. I don't want to hype it too much for you, but I am confident you won't be disappointed. 

My only regret is that when I first ordered the game, I didn't order "rook city" and "infernal relics" at the same time (they were available in the same online shop I bought the core game). And now I am having problems finding them... The guys in shop4de have told me that they expect to restock in a couple of weeks, so fingers crossing and obsesive-compulsive checking of their web. 

Ok, I have disgressed a lot! Have fun with the game when you get it!

(And arenson9, btw, how would you rephrase 'online spanish store' to make it sound more natural for a native English speaker? I am trying but I can't :( - And my English is supposed to be sooo much better that my German, so go figure! )

posts.name: arenson9
posts.cooked:
Wendell:

(And arenson9, btw, how would you rephrase 'online spanish store' to make it sound more natural for a native English speaker? … ) 

I think this is less of an issue about native vs. non-native speakers and more of an issue of ambiguity of meaning.

Spanish can refer either to the Spanish language or to the country of Spain. So what does it mean for a store to be Spanish? Are we saying that the store is in Spain? That it serves a Spanish market? That it sells things that are Spanish? That it uses the Spanish language?

Since the phrase 'online Spanish store' does not have a comma between the two adjectives, it puts more emphasis on the 'Spanish store' than on the 'online store', connotating that the 'Spanish store' is more inseperable than the online store. This serves to emphasize the ambiguity as to what is meant by a 'Spanish store'.

Using a comma (online, Spanish store) or reversing the order (Spanish online store) would help deemphasize the ambiguity of what a 'Spanish store' is, but the ambiguity won't go away unless more words are used to specify what is meant.
